claim: Numerous brain regions have neural correlates of gradually accumulating evidence for decision-making.
source: Numerous brain regions have been shown to have neural correlates of gradually accumulating evidence for decision-making, but the causal roles of these regions in decisions driven by accumulation of evidence have yet to be determined.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact in the field.

claim: The causal roles of brain regions with neural correlates of evidence accumulation have not yet been determined.
source: Numerous brain regions have been shown to have neural correlates of gradually accumulating evidence for decision-making, but the causal roles of these regions in decisions driven by accumulation of evidence have yet to be determined.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Rat frontal orienting fields (FOF) have neural correlates of accumulating evidence.
source: Here, in rats performing an auditory evidence accumulation task, we inactivated the frontal orienting fields (FOF) and posterior parietal cortex (PPC), two rat cortical regions that have neural correlates of accumulating evidence and that have been proposed as central to decision-making.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to Hanks et al., 2015 in the introduction.

claim: Rat posterior parietal cortex (PPC) has neural correlates of accumulating evidence.
source: Here, in rats performing an auditory evidence accumulation task, we inactivated the frontal orienting fields (FOF) and posterior parietal cortex (PPC), two rat cortical regions that have neural correlates of accumulating evidence and that have been proposed as central to decision-making.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to Hanks et al., 2015 in the introduction.

claim: FOF and PPC have been proposed as central to decision-making in rats.
source: Here, in rats performing an auditory evidence accumulation task, we inactivated the frontal orienting fields (FOF) and posterior parietal cortex (PPC), two rat cortical regions that have neural correlates of accumulating evidence and that have been proposed as central to decision-making.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a motivation for studying these regions.

claim: Inactivation of the FOF induced substantial performance impairments in the auditory evidence accumulation task.
source: Inactivation of the FOF induced substantial performance impairments that were quantitatively best described as an impairment in the output pathway of an evidence accumulator with a long integration time constant (>240 ms).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: FOF inactivation impairments are best described as an impairment in the output pathway of an evidence accumulator with a long integration time constant (>240 ms).
source: Inactivation of the FOF induced substantial performance impairments that were quantitatively best described as an impairment in the output pathway of an evidence accumulator with a long integration time constant (>240 ms).
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the FOF inactivation experiments, supported by model-based analysis in Figure 4.

claim: PPC plays a minimal role in decisions guided by accumulating auditory evidence.
source: In contrast, we found a minimal role for PPC in decisions guided by accumulating auditory evidence, even while finding a strong role for PPC in internally-guided decisions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 7 and 9.

claim: PPC plays a strong role in internally-guided decisions.
source: In contrast, we found a minimal role for PPC in decisions guided by accumulating auditory evidence, even while finding a strong role for PPC in internally-guided decisions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by free-choice trial data in Figure 9.

claim: Gradual accumulation of evidence has been implicated in value-based decisions.
source: Gradual accumulation of evidence for or against different choices has been implicated in many types of decision-making, including value-based decisions (Basten et al., 2010; Milosavljevic et al., 2010; Cavanagh et al., 2011; Hunt et al., 2012; Solway and Botvinick, 2012), social decisions (Krajbich and Rangel, 2011), economic decisions (Gluth et al., 2012), gambling decisions (Busemeyer and Townsend, 1993), memory-based decisions (Ratcliff, 1978), numerical comparison decisions (Sigman and Dehaene, 2005), visual search decisions (Purcell et al., 2010; Heitz and Schall, 2012), and perceptual (Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Ratcliff et al., 2007; Mante et al., 2013) decisions.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Gradual accumulation of evidence is considered a core decision-making process.
source: It is therefore considered a core decision-making process.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the breadth of decision types involving evidence accumulation.

claim: Neural correlates of evidence accumulation have been reported in primate PPC.
source: Although neural correlates of evidence accumulation have been reported in several interconnected primate brain regions—such as PPC (Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; Hunt et al., 2012), prefrontal cortex (Hunt et al., 2012) including frontal eye fields (FEF; Kim and Shadlen, 1999; Purcell et al., 2010; Ding and Gold, 2012; Heitz and Schall, 2012; Mante et al., 2013), striatum (Ding and Gold, 2010), and superior colliculus (Horwitz and Newsome, 1999; Ratcliff et al., 2007)—the specific roles of these different brain regions in decisions driven by accumulation of evidence have not yet been distinguished.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; and Hunt et al., 2012.

claim: Neural correlates of evidence accumulation have been reported in primate prefrontal cortex.
source: Although neural correlates of evidence accumulation have been reported in several interconnected primate brain regions—such as PPC (Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; Hunt et al., 2012), prefrontal cortex (Hunt et al., 2012) including frontal eye fields (FEF; Kim and Shadlen, 1999; Purcell et al., 2010; Ding and Gold, 2012; Heitz and Schall, 2012; Mante et al., 2013), striatum (Ding and Gold, 2010), and superior colliculus (Horwitz and Newsome, 1999; Ratcliff et al., 2007)—the specific roles of these different brain regions in decisions driven by accumulation of evidence have not yet been distinguished.

evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: The Poisson Clicks task allows detailed quantitative modeling of the accumulation and decision processes.
source: We recently developed a rat model of gradual accumulation of evidence for decision-making, using a task that allows detailed quantitative modeling of the accumulation and decision processes ('Poisson Clicks' task; Brunton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a property of the task and supported by citation to Brunton et al., 2013.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings in rat PPC revealed classic neural correlates of evidence accumulation.
source: In separate work from our laboratory using the Poisson Clicks task, electrophysiological recordings in rat PPC and Frontal Orienting Fields (FOF; Erlich et al., 2011) revealed classic neural correlates of evidence accumulation (Figure 1 of Hanks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hanks et al., 2015.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings in rat FOF revealed classic neural correlates of evidence accumulation.
source: In separate work from our laboratory using the Poisson Clicks task, electrophysiological recordings in rat PPC and Frontal Orienting Fields (FOF; Erlich et al., 2011) revealed classic neural correlates of evidence accumulation (Figure 1 of Hanks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hanks et al., 2015.

claim: Neurons in rat PPC and FOF ramp up their activity during the stimulus, with the slope correlated with the strength of momentary evidence.
source: Specifically, we found neurons in these rat regions that ramp up their activity during the stimulus, and the slope of that ramp is correlated with the strength of the momentary evidence just as one would expect from neurons whose firing rates represent the accumulation of evidence over time, and just as previously reported in monkey regions that have been suggested as analogous to the rat PPC and FOF (primate PPC: Shadlen and Newsome, 1996, 2001; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; and monkey FEF: Ding and Gold, 2012; Mante et al., 2013; for PPC analogy, see Whitlock et al., 2008; Reep and Corwin, 2009; Wilber et al., 2014; for FOF/FEF analogy see Erlich et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hanks et al., 2015 and analogous findings in primates.

claim: Rat FOF has delay activity that correlates with short-term memory.
source: The rat FOF has delay activity that correlates with short-term memory, and plays a causal role in short-term memory for future orienting responses (Erlich et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Erlich et al., 2011.

claim: Rat FOF plays a causal role in short-term memory for future orienting responses.
source: The rat FOF has delay activity that correlates with short-term memory, and plays a causal role in short-term memory for future orienting responses (Erlich et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Erlich et al., 2011.

claim: Rat FOF receives inputs from multiple sensory cortices.
source: Furthermore, the rat FOF is well-situated to play an important role in perceptual decision-making, since it receives inputs from multiple sensory cortices (Condé et al., 1995), and it projects to the superior colliculus (SC; Stuesse and Newman, 1990), a subcortical region that, in both rodents and primates, is involved in controlling orienting motions (Isa and Sasaki, 2002; Felsen and Mainen, 2008) and is thought to be involved in decisions reported through such orienting motions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Condé et al., 1995.

claim: Rat FOF projects to the superior colliculus.
source: Furthermore, the rat FOF is well-situated to play an important role in perceptual decision-making, since it receives inputs from multiple sensory cortices (Condé et al., 1995), and it projects to the superior colliculus (SC; Stuesse and Newman, 1990), a subcortical region that, in both rodents and primates, is involved in controlling orienting motions (Isa and Sasaki, 2002; Felsen and Mainen, 2008) and is thought to be involved in decisions reported through such orienting motions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stuesse and Newman, 1990.

claim: The superior colliculus is involved in controlling orienting motions in both rodents and primates.
source: Furthermore, the rat FOF is well-situated to play an important role in perceptual decision-making, since it receives inputs from multiple sensory cortices (Condé et al., 1995), and it projects to the superior colliculus (SC; Stuesse and Newman, 1990), a subcortical region that, in both rodents and primates, is involved in controlling orienting motions (Isa and Sasaki, 2002; Felsen and Mainen, 2008) and is thought to be involved in decisions reported through such orienting motions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Isa and Sasaki, 2002 and Felsen and Mainen, 2008.

claim: The superior colliculus is thought to be involved in decisions reported through orienting motions.
source: Furthermore, the rat FOF is well-situated to play an important role in perceptual decision-making, since it receives inputs from multiple sensory cortices (Condé et al., 1995), and it projects to the superior colliculus (SC; Stuesse and Newman, 1990), a subcortical region that, in both rodents and primates, is involved in controlling orienting motions (Isa and Sasaki, 2002; Felsen and Mainen, 2008) and is thought to be involved in decisions reported through such orienting motions.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the SC's role in orienting motions.

claim: Rat FOF is reciprocally connected with rat PPC.
source: Moreover, the rat FOF is reciprocally connected with the rat PPC (Reep et al., 1987, 1994), which is currently considered a critical, central node in rodent perceptual decision-making (Carandini and Churchland, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reep et al., 1987, 1994.

claim: Rodent PPC is currently considered a critical, central node in rodent perceptual decision-making.
source: Moreover, the rat FOF is reciprocally connected with the rat PPC (Reep et al., 1987, 1994), which is currently considered a critical, central node in rodent perceptual decision-making (Carandini and Churchland, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carandini and Churchland, 2013.

claim: Rodent PPC has delay activity that correlates with performance on short-term memory tasks.
source: The rodent PPC itself also has neural correlates of accumulating evidence (Hanks et al., 2015), and it shares with the FOF some of the key properties that suggest a causal role in decisions driven by accumulation of evidence. The rodent PPC has delay activity that correlates with performance on short-term memory tasks (Nakamura, 1999; Harvey et al., 2012), and, as shown through inactivations, plays a causal role in short-term memory for orienting acts (Harvey et al., 2012) and like FOF receives input from many sensory cortices as well as top-down input from prefrontal cortex, including FOF (Wilber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakamura, 1999 and Harvey et al., 2012.

claim: Rodent PPC plays a causal role in short-term memory for orienting acts.
source: The rodent PPC itself also has neural correlates of accumulating evidence (Hanks et al., 2015), and it shares with the FOF some of the key properties that suggest a causal role in decisions driven by accumulation of evidence. The rodent PPC has delay activity that correlates with performance on short-term memory tasks (Nakamura, 1999; Harvey et al., 2012), and, as shown through inactivations, plays a causal role in short-term memory for orienting acts (Harvey et al., 2012) and like FOF receives input from many sensory cortices as well as top-down input from prefrontal cortex, including FOF (Wilber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harvey et al., 2012.

claim: Rodent PPC receives input from many sensory cortices.
source: The rodent PPC itself also has neural correlates of accumulating evidence (Hanks et al., 2015), and it shares with the FOF some of the key properties that suggest a causal role in decisions driven by accumulation of evidence. The rodent PPC has delay activity that correlates with performance on short-term memory tasks (Nakamura, 1999; Harvey et al., 2012), and, as shown through inactivations, plays a causal role in short-term memory for orienting acts (Harvey et al., 2012) and like FOF receives input from many sensory cortices as well as top-down input from prefrontal cortex, including FOF (Wilber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilber et al., 2014.

claim: Rodent PPC receives top-down input from prefrontal cortex, including FOF.
source: The rodent PPC itself also has neural correlates of accumulating evidence (Hanks et al., 2015), and it shares with the FOF some of the key properties that suggest a causal role in decisions driven by accumulation of evidence. The rodent PPC has delay activity that correlates with performance on short-term memory tasks (Nakamura, 1999; Harvey et al., 2012), and, as shown through inactivations, plays a causal role in short-term memory for orienting acts (Harvey et al., 2012) and like FOF receives input from many sensory cortices as well as top-down input from prefrontal cortex, including FOF (Wilber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilber et al., 2014.

claim: FOF and PPC are the most prominent candidate regions in rodent association cortex for being important nodes in orienting decisions guided by accumulation of evidence.
source: For these reasons, the FOF and the PPC are the most prominent candidate regions in rodent association cortex for being important nodes in orienting decisions guided by accumulation of evidence. We focus on these two areas here.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the properties of these regions described in the introduction.

claim: Bilateral cannula were implanted in both FOF and PPC of rats trained to perform the Poisson Clicks task.
source: We implanted bilateral cannula in both FOF and PPC of rats trained to perform the Poisson Clicks task, and inactivated these regions with the GABA-A agonist muscimol while the rats performed the task.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: FOF and PPC were inactivated with the GABA-A agonist muscimol.
source: We implanted bilateral cannula in both FOF and PPC of rats trained to perform the Poisson Clicks task, and inactivated these regions with the GABA-A agonist muscimol while the rats performed the task.
evidence: This describes the method of inactivation used in the study.

claim: Quantitative modeling was used to characterize which aspect of the accumulation and decision process was impacted by FOF inactivation.
source: Consistent with expectations drawn from neural correlates in the rat FOF, inactivation of the FOF impaired performance in the task. We used quantitative modeling to characterize which aspect of the accumulation and decision process was impacted by inactivation of the FOF.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used to interpret the FOF inactivation results.

claim: The behavioral impairment caused by FOF infusions could be parsimoniously and quantitatively explained as an impairment in the premotor output pathway of an evidence accumulator with a long accumulation time constant (240 ms or more).
source: The results of these analyses revealed a specific location for the FOF in the causal circuit underlying the Poisson Clicks behavior: the behavioral impairment caused by FOF infusions could be parsimoniously and quantitatively explained as an impairment in the premotor output pathway of an evidence accumulator with a long accumulation time constant (240 ms or more).
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the FOF inactivation experiments, supported by model-based analysis.

claim: It is possible that the decision itself (i.e., the categorization of the graded accumulator value into a discrete choice) could occur in the FOF.
source: It is possible that the decision itself (i.e., the categorization of the graded accumulator value into a discrete choice, which is a process subsequent to graded evidence accumulation) could occur in the FOF.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative possibility based on the results.

claim: PPC inactivations had a relatively minor effect on the Poisson Clicks task.
source: In contrast, we found that PPC inactivations had a relatively minor effect on the Poisson Clicks task.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding and supported by data in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: PPC inactivations had strong effects on interleaved 'free-choice' trials.
source: This was true even while the same PPC inactivations had strong effects on interleaved 'free-choice' trials, in which no sensory evidence was provided and rats were rewarded regardless of their choice of response.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding and supported by data in Figure 9.

claim: The PPC plays a minimal causal role in decisions guided by accumulation of auditory evidence.
source: Our data thus suggest that the PPC plays a minimal causal role in decisions guided by accumulation of auditory evidence, while playing an important role in internally-guided decisions.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the PPC inactivation results.

claim: The PPC plays an important role in internally-guided decisions.
source: Our data thus suggest that the PPC plays a minimal causal role in decisions guided by accumulation of auditory evidence, while playing an important role in internally-guided decisions.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the free-choice trial results.

claim: The findings from inactivations of the PPC and the FOF provide important constraints on the neural circuitry underlying decisions guided by accumulation of auditory evidence in the rat.
source: Together, our findings from inactivations of the PPC and the FOF provide important constraints on the neural circuitry underlying decisions guided by accumulation of auditory evidence in the rat.
evidence: This is stated as the overall significance of the study.

claim: 14 male Long-Evans rats were trained on the Poisson Clicks accumulation task.
source: We trained male Long-Evans rats (n = 14 rats) on the Poisson Clicks accumulation task (Figure 1, Brunton et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the subjects and task used in the study.

claim: On accumulation trials, rats learned to report which side had played the greater total number of clicks by nose-poking into the corresponding side port.
source: The rats learned to report which side had played the greater total number of clicks by nose-poking into the corresponding side port (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the behavioral task and is illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: For very easy trials (large click differences) performance is approximately 90% correct.
source: For very easy trials (large click differences) performance is ≈90% correct.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The median accumulation time constant across rats was 810 ms.
source: The median (810 ms) is marked by a thin gray line.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Rats' performance increases with longer duration stimuli, consistent with an accumulation strategy.
source: The rats' performance increases with longer duration stimuli, consistent with an accumulation strategy.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Clicks throughout the stimulus were used in the rats' decision process.
source: Reverse correlation analyses showing that clicks throughout the stimulus were used in the rats' decision process, supporting the long accumulation time constants in (B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The accumulator model uses 9 parameters to transform the stimulus on each trial into a probability distribution about the choice of the rat.
source: The accumulator model uses 9-parameters (described in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) to transform the stimulus on each trial (input to the model as the left and right click times) into a probability distribution about the choice of the rat.
evidence: This describes the model used for analysis and is detailed in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bilateral infusion of muscimol into the FOF results in a substantial impairment on accumulation trials.
source: Bilateral infusion of muscimol into the FOF results in a substantial impairment on accumulation trials but has no effect on side LED trials.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Bilateral FOF inactivation has no effect on side LED trials.
source: Bilateral infusion of muscimol into the FOF results in a substantial impairment on accumulation trials but has no effect on side LED trials.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Unilateral infusion of muscimol into the FOF results in a profound ipsilateral bias on accumulation trials.
source: Unilateral infusion of muscimol into the FOF results in a profound ipsilateral bias on accumulation trials but has no effect on side LED trials.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Unilateral FOF inactivation has no effect on side LED trials.
source: Unilateral infusion of muscimol into the FOF results in a profound ipsilateral bias on accumulation trials but has no effect on side LED trials.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Bilateral FOF inactivations reduced the subjects' accumulation time constant from approximately +0.8 s to approximately -0.24 s.
source: For data from bilateral inactivation sessions, the maximum likelihood parameter values (center of blue likelihood peak, Figure 4B) changed significantly. The inactivation data now had a dramatically different and much shorter accumulation time constant of the opposite sign to the control data, τ ≈ −0.24 s (leaky accumulation over only a quarter of a second).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: After bilateral FOF inactivation, the best-fitting lapse rate remained essentially unchanged from control.
source: In contrast, the best-fitting lapse rate remained essentially unchanged from control.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The post-categorization bias model best fit the experimental data from unilateral FOF inactivations.
source: Of these four models, the one that best fit the experimental data was (a), the post-categorization bias model in which the FOF is part of the output pathway of the accumulator (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The best-fit value of κ contralateral to the FOF inactivation was 0.52.
source: The value of κ contralateral to the inactivation (κC) that best fit the data was 0.52, suggesting that on over 50% of trials rats reversed their contra-choices to ipsi-choices.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the model fitting.

claim: Unilateral PPC inactivations resulted in a small effect that was approximately 10× smaller than the effect in the FOF.
source: Surprisingly, our unilateral PPC inactivations resulted in a small effect that was ≈10× smaller than the effect in the FOF.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between FOF and PPC inactivation effects.

claim: The average ipsilateral bias from unilateral PPC inactivations was 4.2 ± 2.4% (mean ± s.e.).
source: The average ipsilateral bias was 4.2 ± 2.4% (mean ± s.e.) (Figure 7A; t-test t13 = 1.76, p > 0.1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Bilateral PPC inactivation produced a very small but significant 3.6% decrease in performance on accumulation trials.
source: During the bilateral PPC inactivation sessions there was a very small but significant 3.6% decrease in performance on accumulation trials (Figure 7B, p < 0.02 vs isoflurane, GLMM test).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Unilateral PPC inactivations produced a very strong and reliable ipsilateral bias on free choice trials.
source: In remarkable parallel to Wilke et al.'s results in primates, unilateral PPC inactivations (300 ng of muscimol) during free-choice sessions produced a very strong and reliable ipsilateral bias on free choice trials (Figure 9B,C; t-test t26 = 3.70, p = 0.001).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 9B,C.

claim: Unilateral PPC inactivations produced no ipsilateral bias on intermixed accumulation trials.
source: The strong ipsilateral bias in free choice trials was observed even while, consistent with our previous PPC inactivations, there was no ipsilateral bias on the intermixed accumulation trials (t-test t26 = −0.99, p = 0.329) nor on the Side LED trials (t-test t8 = 1.42, p = 0.194; Figure 9C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Simultaneous bilateral FOF and unilateral PPC inactivations produced a significant 15.1% bias ipsilateral to the side of the PPC infusion.
source: To probe whether inactivation of the FOF could reveal an effect of PPC inactivation, we bilaterally inactivated the FOF while simultaneously infusing 300 ng of muscimol unilaterally into the PPC. This combination of infusions produced a significant 15.1% bias ipsilateral to the side of the PPC infusion (Figure 9E, p < 0.0012, GLMM test).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 9E.

claim: During auditory evidence accumulation the PPC may have a real but weak influence on choice that is normally overridden by a stronger signal from the FOF.
source: The data furthermore suggest that during auditory evidence accumulation the PPC may have a real but weak influence on choice that is normally overridden by a stronger signal from the FOF.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the combined FOF+PPC inactivation results.

claim: The FOF is either directly involved in the process of accumulating evidence, or is a requisite component in the output pathway of an accumulator with a long time constant.
source: These results indicate that the FOF is either (a) itself directly involved in the process of accumulating evidence, and the inactivations made the accumulator leaky; or (b) the FOF is a requisite component in the output pathway of an accumulator with a long time constant, that is, the FOF is part of the chain of regions that transform evidence accumulated with a time-constant longer than 0.24 s into an orienting decision.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the bilateral FOF inactivation results.

claim: The FOF is part of the output pathway of the accumulator, perhaps part of computing or representing the animal's discrete choice after having categorized the accumulator value.
source: Our results in rat FOF are consistent with those of Gold and Shadlen, but go considerably further in specifically suggesting the FOF as a requisite premotor component of the output pathway of a long time constant (>0.24 s) evidence accumulator.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the unilateral FOF inactivation model-based analysis.

claim: Decisions with shorter processing times may involve circuits that bypass the FOF.
source: Such decisions, including perhaps decisions that require auditory evidence accumulation over only short times (<0.24 s), may depend on pathways that bypass the FOF, perhaps involving direct connections from auditory cortex to the striatum (Znamenskiy and Zador, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the FOF results and supported by citation.

claim: Neither FOF nor PPC appears likely to play a major causal role in the gradual evidence accumulation process per se.
source: Neither region appears likely to play a major causal role in the gradual evidence accumulation process per se.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: Animal use procedures were approved by the Princeton University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: Animal use procedures were approved by the Princeton University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and carried out in accordance with National Institutes of Health standards.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All subjects were male Long-Evans rats from Taconic, NY.
source: All subjects were male Long-Evans rats (Taconic, NY).
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: Rats were placed on a restricted water schedule to motivate them to work for water reward.
source: Rats were placed on a restricted water schedule to motivate them to work for water reward.
evidence: This describes the motivation method used in the study.

claim: The fixation period duration was 2 s for all accumulation trials.
source: The duration of fixation was 2 s for all accumulation trials.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the behavioral task.

claim: The total generative click rate (left + right rate) was held constant at 40 clicks/s.
source: The total generative click rate (left + right rate) was held constant at 40 clicks/s, and trial difficulty was controlled by adjusting the relative left vs right rates, as well as the duration of the stimulus.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the behavioral task.

claim: Single-sided trials used clicks played at a Poisson rate of 100 Hz from one speaker.
source: A single-sided trial was much like an accumulation trial, but all the clicks came from one speaker and were played at a Poisson rate of 100 Hz.
evidence: This describes a control trial type used in the study.

claim: Side LED trials comprised approximately 10% of the total trials.
source: The right and left side LED trials, together, comprised ≈10% of the total trials.
evidence: This describes the proportion of control trials in the task.

claim: Free-choice trials comprised 25% of trials in free-choice sessions.
source: We randomly intermixed 25% free choice trials with 65% accumulation trials and 10% Side LED trials (Figure 9A).
evidence: This describes the trial composition in free-choice sessions.

claim: A total of 26,521 trials from 161 infusions into the FOF and PPC of 14 rats were analyzed.
source: We report the results of five different types of inactivations: unilateral FOF, bilateral FOF, unilateral PPC, bilateral PPC, and combined bilateral FOF + unilateral PPC inactivations, for a total of 26,521 trials from 161 infusions into the FOF and PPC of 14 rats (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the total amount of data collected in the study.

claim: The initial bilateral FOF inactivation used 300 ng of muscimol per side, which prevented rats from performing the task.
source: For the first bilateral FOF inactivation session we infused 300 ng of muscimol per side, for a total of 600 ng. After these infusions rats did not perform the task.
evidence: This describes a dose-finding result from the study.

claim: Bilateral FOF inactivations used 75 ng of muscimol per side.
source: We subsequently used a smaller dose of 75 ng per side (Note: this is half the dose used in the bilateral PPC experiment described below).
evidence: This describes the dose used for bilateral FOF inactivations.

claim: Bilateral FOF inactivation (75 ng per side) resulted in a significant 10.3% decrement on performance on accumulation trials.
source: This resulted in a significant 10.3% decrement on performance on accumulation trials (p = 0.018, GLMM test; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The ipsilateral bias from unilateral FOF infusions was 52 ± 7% (mean ± s.e.) for accumulation trials.
source: Averaged across all unilateral FOF infusion sessions, the ipsilateral bias (defined as ipsilateral % correct − contralateral % correct), was 52 ± 7% (mean ± s.e.) for accumulation trials (t-test across 12 rats t11 = 7.27, p < 10−4; two rats in group 3 failed to perform sufficient numbers of trials during FOF inactivations to be included in this analysis).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative result from unilateral FOF inactivations.

claim: 87% (26/30) of individual FOF infusion sessions resulted in a positive ipsilateral bias.
source: The ipsilateral bias induced by FOF inactivation was highly reproducible: 87% (26/30) of individual infusion sessions resulted in a positive ipsilateral bias (sign-test, p < 0.001), and in every single rat there were more rightward responses after rightward infusions than leftward infusions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Unilateral FOF inactivations had no significant effect on side LED trials.
source: Importantly, as in the bilateral inactivations, there was no significant effect on side LED trials (t-test t5 = 1.55, p > 0.15; Figure 3C, side LED Trials), nor did unilateral FOF inactivations have an effect on the response time on side LED trials (repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,3) = 0.65, p > 0.4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: FOF inactivations produced no observable effects outside of the behavioral task.
source: Furthermore, the inactivations produced no observable effects outside of the behavioral task. Infused animals appeared normal in their home cages both immediately after the infusion and after the behavioral session.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: Based on bootstrapping analysis, only two parameters shifted significantly from control data after bilateral FOF inactivation: λ and Þ.
source: To further validate these results we resampled the trials (with replacement) and refit the model on the resampled trials 300 times. Based on this analysis, only two parameters shifted significantly from the control data: λ (95% C.I. = [−7.91 −1.31]; control value was 1.22) and Þ (95% C.I. = [0.10 1.50]; control value was 0.065).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the bootstrapping analysis.

claim: The change in λ after bilateral FOF inactivation is both significant and substantial.
source: The change in λ is both significant and substantial, and accounts for most of the change in performance.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the bootstrapping results.

claim: The change in decision boundary Þ after bilateral FOF inactivation is significant but very small.
source: The change in decision boundary, Þ (pronounced 'sho') is significant but very small, corresponding a horizontal shift in the psychometric curve of only one click.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the bootstrapping results.

claim: According to BIC, the 1-parameter λ model is more likely than the full 9-parameter model for bilateral FOF data.
source: According to BIC, the 1-parameter model is the more likely model, supporting the idea that the major effect of bilateral FOF inactivation was a change in the time constant of accumulation (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 2.

claim: Leave-one-session-out cross validation found a significant main effect of model on likelihood/trial for unilateral FOF inactivations.
source: We verified that the post-categorization model was best by using a leave-one-session-out cross validation. For each of the 30 unilateral FOF infusion sessions, we fit the 4 models to the 29 other sessions and then evaluated the likelihood of the fit on the left-out session. Using this approach we found a significant main effect of model on likelihood/trial (repeated-measures ANOVA F(3,87) = 10.76, p < 10−5) and Bonferroni-Holm corrected post-hoc t-tests reveal that all models were significantly different from each other (p < 0.005) except the noise and accumulator shift models (p > 0.4).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the cross-validation analysis.

claim: Using the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, four parameters changed significantly from control values in the 8-parameter model of unilateral FOF inactivation.
source: With 40,000 samples of this 8 dimensional distribution (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), we estimate that four parameters changed significantly from their control values. First, accumulator noise increased from 5 × 10−4 to 0.746 (95% C.I. = [0.125 12.123], p = 10−4), which is still a small value and would have a negligible impact on behavioral performance. Second, accumulator shift changed from 0.065 to 0.323 ([0.136 0.890], p = 0.013), which would also have a minimal effect on overall reward rate. Third, κI, the changes from ipsi to contra choices decreased from 0.102 to 0.029 ([0.002 0.071], p = 10−4). Finally, supporting our earlier analysis, κC, increased from 0 to 0.498 ([0.176 0.536], p < 10−3) which results in a very substantial behavioral impact, since this sets the asymptotic performance on the easiest contralateral trials to ≈50%.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the Metropolis-Hastings sampling and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The 1-parameter post-categorization model has the lowest AIC and BIC for unilateral FOF inactivation data.
source: Using AIC and BIC we find that the increase in likelihood is too small to justify the increase in number of parameters.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 3.

claim: There was no correlation between dose and bias magnitude in PPC infusions on accumulation trials.
source: There was no correlation between dose and bias magnitude in our PPC infusions on accumulation trials (Figure 8, yellow squares; p > 0.09), strongly contrasting with the significant correlation between dose of muscimol infused into the FOF and bias on accumulation trials (accumulation trials r = 0.85, p < 10−9; Figure 8, magenta squares).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8.

claim: There was a significant correlation between dose of muscimol infused into the FOF and bias on accumulation trials (r = 0.85, p < 10−9).
source: There was no correlation between dose and bias magnitude in our PPC infusions on accumulation trials (Figure 8, yellow squares; p > 0.09), strongly contrasting with the significant correlation between dose of muscimol infused into the FOF and bias on accumulation trials (accumulation trials r = 0.85, p < 10−9; Figure 8, magenta squares).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8.

claim: 85% (23/27) of individual rat PPC inactivation sessions produced an increased fraction of ipsilateral free choices compared to preceding control days.
source: The free-choice bias was highly reproducible: 85% (23/27, sign-test, p < 0.001) individual rat PPC inactivation sessions produced an increased fraction of ipsilateral free choices when compared to free choices on immediately preceding control days (see Figure 9B for an example of PPC infusions that were selected to 'push' the rats away from their innate preference seen on the day before and the day after the infusion).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Inactivation of FOF induced an ipsilateral bias on free choice trials (t-test, t24 = 3.86, p = 0.001).
source: Inactivation of FOF, like the PPC, also induced an ipsilateral bias on free choice trials (t-test, t24 = 3.86, p = 0.001).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 9D.

claim: FOF inactivations in free-choice sessions continued to produce an ipsilateral bias on accumulation trials (t-test t24 = 4.85, p < 0.001).
source: Consistent with our previous experiments, FOF inactivations in free-choice sessions continued to produce an ipsilateral bias on accumulation trials (t-test t24 = 4.85, p < 0.001) but not on side LED trials (t-test t18 = 1.65, p = 0.117; Figure 9D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The rat PPC and FOF have been suggested as analogous to primate PPC and FEF, respectively.
source: Based on a number of criteria, the rat PPC and FOF have been suggested as analogous to the primate PPC and FEF, respectively (Kolb and Walkey, 1987; Reep and Corwin, 2009; Erlich et al., 2011), and accumulation of evidence signals very similar to those in primates have been found in these two rat areas (Hanks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: In memory-guided saccade tasks, LIP inactivations have no effect on the choice of saccading either towards or away from the correct hemifield.
source: In memory-guided saccade tasks, LIP inactivations have no effect on the choice of saccading either towards or away from the correct hemifield (Chafee and Goldman-Rakic, 2000; Wardak et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2010; Wilke et al., 2012), while FEF and prefrontal inactivations reliably generate profound ipsilateral choice biases (Sommer and Tehovnik, 1997; Dias and Segraves, 1999; Chafee and Goldman-Rakic, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: FEF and prefrontal inactivations reliably generate profound ipsilateral choice biases in memory-guided saccade tasks.
source: In memory-guided saccade tasks, LIP inactivations have no effect on the choice of saccading either towards or away from the correct hemifield (Chafee and Goldman-Rakic, 2000; Wardak et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2010; Wilke et al., 2012), while FEF and prefrontal inactivations reliably generate profound ipsilateral choice biases (Sommer and Tehovnik, 1997; Dias and Segraves, 1999; Chafee and Goldman-Rakic, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: In a covert visual search task, LIP inactivation has no effect on error rates.
source: Similarly, in a covert visual search task, LIP inactivation has no effect on error rates (Wardak et al., 2002), while inactivation of the FEF generates significant increase in error rates for contralateral targets (Wardak et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Wardak et al., 2002.

claim: Inactivation of the FEF generates significant increase in error rates for contralateral targets in a covert visual search task.
source: Similarly, in a covert visual search task, LIP inactivation has no effect on error rates (Wardak et al., 2002), while inactivation of the FEF generates significant increase in error rates for contralateral targets (Wardak et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Wardak et al., 2006.

claim: In a memory-guided task with distractors, Suzuki and Gottlieb found no errors after LIP inactivations while finding significant contralateral errors after prefrontal cortex inactivations.
source: Again similarly, in a memory-guided task with distractors, Suzuki and Gottlieb, (2013) found no errors after LIP inactivations while finding significant contralateral errors after prefrontal cortex inactivations.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Suzuki and Gottlieb, 2013.

claim: Microstimulation of primate FEF during an accumulation of evidence task led Gold and Shadlen to conclude that 'developing oculomotor commands may reflect the formation of the monkey's direction judgement'.
source: There has been one perturbation study in the primate FEF during an accumulation of evidence task (Gold and Shadlen, 2000). This microstimulation study concluded that 'developing oculomotor commands may reflect the formation of the monkey's direction judgement' (i.e., its decision).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Gold and Shadlen, 2000.

claim: Microstimulation of LIP in a reaction time Random Dots task produced results that could be quantitatively explained if the microstimulation added a small constant offset to the value of the accumulator.
source: There has been one perturbation study in the primate PPC during an accumulation of evidence task (Hanks et al., 2006). This microstimulation study used a reaction time version of the Random Dots task, and found a pattern of results following LIP microstimulation that could be quantitatively explained in an accumulation-to-bound model if the microstimulation added a small constant offset to the value of the accumulator (Hanks et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Hanks et al., 2006.

claim: Microstimulation may activate axon terminals or fibers of passage.
source: An alternative possibility, noted in their discussion (Hanks et al., 2006), and which would reconcile our results with theirs, is that microstimulation may activate axon terminals or fibers of passage (Histed et al., 2009, 2013; but see Tehovnik and Slocum, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Muscimol does not affect axons or fibers of passage.
source: Since muscimol does not affect axons or fibers of passage, this possibility would be consistent with our data.
evidence: This is stated as a property of muscimol that distinguishes it from microstimulation.

claim: Accumulation signals are correlated with confidence.
source: Accumulation signals are also correlated with confidence (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Komura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The accumulation signals observed in the PPC may be used for computing choice confidence rather than driving choice behavior.
source: One possibility is that, instead of being used to drive choice behavior, the accumulation signals observed in the PPC are used for computing choice confidence (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a speculative possibility in the Discussion.

claim: Confidence could be part of a process for optimizing behavior over many trials.
source: Confidence could be part of a process for optimizing behavior over many trials, or, in a reaction time version of the task, confidence could be part of determining when the subject chooses to commit to a decision.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative possibility in the Discussion.

claim: In a reaction time version of the task, confidence could be part of determining when the subject chooses to commit to a decision.
source: Confidence could be part of a process for optimizing behavior over many trials, or, in a reaction time version of the task, confidence could be part of determining when the subject chooses to commit to a decision.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative possibility in the Discussion.
